en: Külchoro, lion of the wilds,
Did not so much as grunt when the spear struck.
If struck by a battle-axe, the fierce one
Would never budge from his place.
He stood firm and paid it no heed,
Counting Ümötöy’s thrust
As nothing beside his boot-heel.
The Lord Most High had granted the companion
Valor and lionheartedness
Beyond all measure.
His fortune was complete;
That Külchoro was a true warrior.
He took no account of high or low;
Such was his heroism
That he gave no thought to dying.
He turned the mouth of Surkoën,
The broad-rumped, mattock-hoofed steed
He rode into battle.
“How many more tricks have you, hero?
If your own strength is not enough,
Call all your Kazakhs,” he said,
And stood laughing boldly.
Ümötöy of the Kazakhs
Thrust not once but ten times,
Reeling there like a slave.
Though he struck twenty times, Külchoro paid no heed,
Counting it as nothing beside his boot-heel.
The lion Külchoro stood and said:
“By your father’s grave, Ümötöy,
It seems you have no sense at all.
Put aside this frenzy.
Your strength alone cannot prevail;
Bring on your strongest men—
Your excited Kazakhs, your nation of ten thousand.
Fire your heavy muskets and draw your bows;
If you have the strength, slaughter me.
Do not prance about, Kazakh host;
Stop, or you will be scattered.
You came as a guest, yet stand there bristling;
Do not stir up a bitter quarrel.
Do not let every last one of you
Perish in a massacre.
Do not push matters to the bitter end,
Lest your survivors say
That I crushed and overwhelmed the dead.
Become a moonless night;
Ümötöy and your two thousand Kazakhs,
Become one with all your people.
When I thrust with wrath boiling,
Would I prosper if I shrank from you,
You vain and teeming Kazakh host?
If the companion feared you,
Would his purpose remain firm?
You thrust your spear at a mediator
And stood there raging.
Can a hero behave like you?
Take care that your head is not shattered;
Would a man prosper by sparing you?
Be on your guard, Ümötöy;
I shall not stand dull-eyed without striking back.
If you call yourself a lord, I am a lord’s son,
One of noble birth.
If you call yourself a khan, I too am a khan’s son.
You rave, Ümötöy—
When was I ever a slave of the Kazakhs,
Living on watery ayran and blue dried curds?
If my anger rises and I stand bristling,
Do not flee in terror,
Crying, ‘Dear brother, mercy, mercy!’
And crawl away to your separate lands.
You are overwrought, Ümötöy;
Do not squander your possessions.
Do not cry, ‘We are dead, dear brother—mercy!’
And do not let your trailing host
Flee toward Sary-Arka!
If the companion stiffens in wrath,
May he not drain the Kazakhs dry;
May your people not grieve,
Crying, ‘God, Almighty God!’
If Külchoro strains his strength,
May he not tear out your very spine;
If he strikes in earnest by chance,
May his spear not suddenly land
And take your entrusted life.
May God not strike my bloodthirsty uncle
For saying, ‘My companion speared my cousin!’
May no one mock us, saying,
‘How wicked they are,
To wage war against blood kin from the same womb!’”
So saying, Külchoro
Still did not strike back or budge,
But turned his stallion’s head.
That formidable lion, with a voice like a trumpet,
Stood there laughing boldly.
Ümötöy, son of Köksö,
Leveled his spear in plain sight.
See the slave’s insolence:
Assaulting the companion,
He struck him again with the spear.
The companion did not even flinch an eyebrow;
Though the teeming Kazakhs thrust their spears,
The noble companion never stirred.
He was the tempered tip of keen steel,
The descendant of Khan Alakö.
Silver-eyed and sun-faced,
A peerless warrior radiant as the sun,
Of a noble father, a warrior vast as the sea.
His fortune was complete;
Could you see within the companion,
It was broader than the face of the earth.
God alone creates life,
And He would never soon grant the world
Another champion of the companion’s stature.
Ümötöy, son of Köksö,
Raised an uproar and launched a raid,
Charging in with his spear.
As though his wife had borne a son,
Without a care in the world,
Your valiant warrior rode laughing.
“Ümötöy of heroic Köksö,
Mark well what I tell you:
Father Ümötöy, stop—or sink into the earth.
I have spoken weighty words; heed me.
Your shield will be torn apart,
And if you will not listen, Kazakh slave,
You yourself will now be shattered.
Great fortune lies in my counsel;
If I charge alone in fury,
Your flesh, Kazakh slave,
Will now be torn to pieces.
I shall unleash my wrath upon you;
If my anger rises and I rear up,
Though you two are honored cousins,
I shall surely strike one of you.”
When Ümötöy kept thrusting,
Then mighty Külchoro
Swelled with wrath and strength;
Upon your princely warrior’s face
Lay ice four fingers thick.
His noble blood boiled fiercely;
Gripping his weapon’s hilt,
His spirit could no longer be restrained.
His countenance was transformed,
His face paled and his heart burned;
Unable to contain himself,
His eyes blazed like fire.
His broad white teeth, like a gateway—
Teeth fit for a stout tethering post—
He ground apart in rage.
When your lion warrior grew impassioned,
He would take his sword in hand;
Though forty ranks of foes should come,
Though strength narrowed his eyes,
Though forty thousand spears struck at once,
That warrior would never flinch,
But leave slaughter in his wake.
When he took the sword in hand,
Such was his terrible prowess—
He unleashed doomsday calamity.
When the warrior grew wrathful,
Blood flowed every way;
Once blood was shed, lives departed,
And he left no living form behind.
Those who approached, that tiger of a man
Swept utterly away.
When Külchoro was enraged,
He brought slaughter upon the age.
He was the leopard, he was the lion,
He was the dark-maned lone wolf.
Külchoro cried out in anger:
“When a warrior comes as an envoy,
Did I say he should be met with wrath,
With shouting and a leveled spear?
Did I say any such thing?
No blood-debt of your seven forefathers is owed;
Blustering Ümötöy,
Have I consumed what you hold dear?
Into your old homeland, Sary-Arka,
Did I send hostile scouts?
Did I slaughter your people in mischief
Or raid and take your horses?
Have I fallen prey to a sly demon?
Ümötöy, son of Khan Köksö,
My wrath has risen and blinded me;
If I attack, you will learn your lesson!
If I rear up in anger,
You will flee all the way to Sary-Arka!
If I charge with a single shout,
You will be crushed to dust!
If I grow wrathful, you will die;
These hands that reached the Kalmyks—
You will now see, Ümötöy,
The true abode from which none return!
You will truly learn your lesson;
If I gather my strength, you will die!
If I regard you as kin,
Wretched Ümötöy,
You will seem no different from those Chinese.
If you are a champion, if you are a lion,
If, finding no mountain to assault,
You think I am someone easily dealt with
And stand there girded for battle,
Then tighten your belt securely.
Seek from the Chinese the blood-price
For your father, heroic Köksö, whom they slew!
Zhylgynduu, Keng-Kol, and broad Talas
Are not the lands of Bakburchun;
The few Argyn and Kyrgyz people
Are not the forty tribes of China.
You shout and level your spear—
This conduct of yours is no innocent thing!
If I rise in wrath,
You will die now, cousin!
Your guilt is on your own head;
Now your deeds will fall upon you!
You will learn what strife is
If you still refuse to listen:
You will wear the very robe of the Chinese.
Beneath the battle standard, your blood
And your lives will spill forth now!
If I join battle fiercely,
Your people will lie slaughtered;
You men who boast of prowess
Will be consumed by grief and care.
Ümötöy, who began this war,
Do not say your teeming people have submitted!”
So saying, Külchoro
Braced himself in anger
And settled firmly in the hollow.
When the mighty warrior grew wrathful,
His fury spread across his face.
Terrifying everyone in sight,
He urged forward his gray horse,
Which flew like a cloud.
He donned his blue mail;
To behold that mighty man,
He seemed ready for any deed,
Preparing himself at an angle.
“If I happen to strike back,
If I unexpectedly join battle,
Will disaster then befall
These wretched Kazakhs?
Will my dear lord Semetey
Shame me, saying, ‘You slaughtered them needlessly’?”
So he wondered.
Thus did Külchoro,
That peerless man, consider what lay ahead,
A man unlike all other men;
So Külchoro stood there that day.
Thinking many thoughts beforehand,
He called out sternly to Ümötöy.
But Ümötöy would not heed restraint,
And there was no reforming him.

At this wretched slave of mine!
